title: Business secretary to meet Jaguar Land Rover boss as thousands of job cuts expected
description: Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the Unite union to discuss the impact of thousands of expecte
body: Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the Unite union to discuss the impact of thousands of expected job cuts at the car maker.JLR confirmed to the BBC it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.The company did not confirm the numbers but the Times reported as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.Reynolds told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the meeting early next week will focus on ways to "mitigate any job losses" but ruled out a bailout for the company.Asked about the cuts, which are believed to impact mainly white collar workers, Reynolds said: "A company the size of JLR, which is a huge British success story, at various times in its business cycle, the number of, directly, people it employs will change."If this is about making sure over time that the workforce is right to make the business as competitive as possible, that's the conversation we need to have."He said there would be no support "if it's to bail people out", but opened the door to a "long-term investment in the future" of the company.The cuts come as Chancellor John Healey is preparing to deliver a speech in the Midlands on Monday promising to boost economic growth by changing how the government values investment in infrastructure such as transport and housing. JLR is based in Coventry, in the West Midlands.The Liberal Democrats said the news would be "devastating" for JLR staff and called for Healey to use his speech to offer "support for those jobs at risk"."This development lays bare that the government's growth mission is falling far short," the party's business spokesperson Sarah Olney said.JLR has not confirmed the scale of the job cuts, but said they would "simplify" the business and "improve efficiency and build greater resilience"."Today, we informed our colleagues, and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business," a spokesperson said."We will share further information with our colleagues first." It did not rule out the prospect of some compulsory redundancies as part of the plans.Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the union had been warning about a "perfect storm" hanging over the automotive industry for some time."Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said.She added there had been "intensive" discussions over the weekend about mitigating jobs losses.Reynolds was asked about the impact on the car industry of the UK's electric vehicle sales target, which means manufacturers must ensure a percentage of the cars they sell each year are zero emissions, with the target rising each year to reach 80% by 2030.He said one of the first things he had done as business secretary was give the industry more flexibility to work towards that and said there was a further consultation open on it."It's not where it needs to be and that's why we're willing to change the regulation to work with where consumer demand is and the industry," he added.He said he had also spoken with West Midlands mayor Richard Parker about supporting the business and its staff.JLR in July said fewer than 300 people would leave the firm under cost savings plans announced at the time.It employs about 30,000 people in its UK operations, with approximately 10,000 people employed at plants overseas.The cyber attack in September 2025 led to the shut down of all manufacturing at JLR for several weeks, meaning not a single vehicle rolled off its production lines.That led to a 27% drop in overall production at the company, which is one of the West Midlands' biggest employers.The overall cost of the cyber-attack and the subsequent loss of manufacturing was estimated to be £1.9bn.In June, the firm announced it planned to cut about £1.7bn in costs over the coming years to help towards its recovery from the attack.JLR had indicated at the time that it would make the savings through cuts in areas such as materials, warranty and fixed costs.Additional reporting by Simon Jack

schema.headline: Business secretary to meet Jaguar Land Rover boss as thousands of job cuts expected

title: Two killed after car hits group of cyclists in Kent
description: Three people have been arrested after a car crashed into a group of cyclists, killing two riders.Kent Police said a white Ford Focus was travelling al
body: Three people have been arrested after a car crashed into a group of cyclists, killing two riders.Kent Police said a white Ford Focus was travelling along Sole Street in Cobham near Gravesend just before 07:50 BST on Sunday when it was involved in a collision with three cyclists.Two of the cyclists - a man in his 60s and woman in her 50s - were confirmed dead by emergency services on the scene, the force added. Their next of kin have been informed. A third cyclist was taken to a local hospital for treatment with minor injuries, according to officers.Two men aged 20 and 21 were arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving. A 19-year-old woman was also detained on suspicion of assisting an offender.Kent Police said the road was closed while an investigation took place. The force is now appealing for anyone who witnessed the incident or saw the car or cyclists before the crash to contact them.Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: Five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
description: An Amazon Air cargo plane overshot the runway while attempting to land at Miami International Airport, killing five people and seriously injuring five
body: An Amazon Air cargo plane overshot the runway while attempting to land at Miami International Airport, killing five people and seriously injuring five more.The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft crashed just before 14:00 local time (19:00 GMT) after departing from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The flight also hit several vehicles on the ground.Amazon said that it is "working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened".All flights were ordered grounded by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) as fire crews raced to the smoking crash site. The crash comes over Labor Day weekend, one of the busiest travel times of the year."At least five people have lost their lives, and five others are injured," Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava said at a news conference on Sunday evening.She added that rescue crews arrived at the scene within "seconds" of the crash. "Right now, our focus is on the families, those who were injured, and the ongoing response," she continued.Three of the five people injured are in critical condition, said Miami Fire Chief Raied Jadallah. The mayor said they were all taken to hospital with "unknown injuries".Several of the injured were trapped inside or under vehicles on the ground, and needed to be extricated by fire and rescue crews, said Jadallah.Officials say it is too early to know the cause of the crash, and that it will be investigated by the National Transportation Safety Board. The federal agency, which investigates all air crashes in the US, plans to hold a news conference on Monday. The Amazon flight operated by 21 Air, a charter company based in North Carolina, "overran Miami International Airport's diagonal runway and is disabled at the northwest end of the airport," the airport said in a statement.Miami Dade Fire Rescue said crews "arrived to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing".The BBC has emailed 21 Air about the incident, but has not received a response.Flight data from tracking site FlightRadar24 shows that the Amazon cargo flight was travelling at 112 knots (129mph, 207km/h) as it exited the "useable runway".In a blog post, the site says the plane came to rest near a parking lot that services an Amazon warehouse and other businesses.There were light thunderstorms and gusting winds in Miami at the time of the incident, the site says.The crash comes during one of the busiest travel weekends of the year in the US.Passengers at Miami International Airport airport told the BBC they were frustrated by the lack of information coming from officials, with many flights cancelled or delayed as a result of the incident. There were long lines at airline counters as people tried to reschedule travel plans, with some saying they would be forced to stay in Miami an extra night.The Transportation Safety Administration (TSA) said there would be 17 million travellers passing through US airports in the week leading up to Monday's Labor Day holiday.The TSA, which screens passengers flying in the US, predicted that 2.3 million people would fly on Sunday alone.

schema.headline: Five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport

title: Russia-Ukraine war: Zelensky expects war to continue after US envoy talks
description: Following rounds of talks on Sunday, which lasted several hours behind closed doors, Zelensky told reporters they had agreed officials from Ukraine, E
body: Following rounds of talks on Sunday, which lasted several hours behind closed doors, Zelensky told reporters they had agreed officials from Ukraine, Europe and America would meet in the near future to continue discussions. He also called for a trilateral meeting with Russia and the US."We're confident there'll be a good resolution here," Witkoff said, adding the negotiators had "made a lot of progress in Moscow", referring to the pair's discussions on Saturday.When asked about the talks in Moscow, Kushner said the US team "went through a lot of the ideas that hadn't worked to date" and "tried to think about" what elements are needed for "durable peace". "It was a very good dialogue, he [Putin] asked a lot of questions, we asked a lot of questions." Witkoff said the envoys had met the Russian leader prior to travelling to Kyiv as they "needed to hear where he stood".Zelensky emphasised that should the war continue into the winter - "which is what it looks like for now" - Ukraine would need air defence and energy support.Ukraine has relied on American-made Patriot interceptors to combat Russian ballistic missiles, but the US has used many of its stockpiles during its war with Iran.In past years, Russia has focused its attacks on energy infrastructure during winter months.  Zelensky said Ukraine needs to develop its own anti-ballistic system, but added the Americans will be increasing production next year, which they are "counting on".

schema.headline: Russia-Ukraine war: Zelensky expects war to continue after US envoy talks

title: Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school
description: As the new school year begins in Austria, a law banning headscarves in schools for girls under 14 has gone into force.The law forbids "traditional Mus
body: As the new school year begins in Austria, a law banning headscarves in schools for girls under 14 has gone into force.The law forbids "traditional Muslim" head coverings, such as hijabs or burkas, in public and private schools across the country.Integration Minister Claudia Bauer, from the conservative People's Party (ÖVP), says the headscarf is "a sign of oppression and a means of controlling girls from the earliest childhood".But critics say the new law is fuelling anti-Muslim feeling in the country and could be unconstitutional.The law was brought in by the conservative-led coalition of three centrist parties, the ÖVP, the Social Democrats (SPÖ) and the liberal Neos. They say the law is a "clear commitment to gender equality" and is intended to protect the rights of young girls.Carla Amina Baghajati, from the official Islamic Community in Austria (IGGÖ), told the BBC that the organisation "firmly opposes the ban"."We believe it unjustifiably restricts the fundamental right to freedom of religion and disproportionately affects Muslim girls," she said."Rather than protecting children, it singles out a specific religious practice and risks excluding the very children it claims to support."The IGGÖ said it would support legal challenges by girls and their families "who believe that their fundamental rights are being infringed" and who wished to bring their cases before the Constitutional Court. The court struck down a previous ban on headscarves in primary schools in 2020 on the basis that it contravened the principle of Austria's religious neutrality.Teachers are expected to enforce the new ban if they see a child wearing a headscarf by holding a series of talks with the student and their legal guardians.If there are repeated violations, child services must be notified and as a last resort, guardians could face fines of up to €800 (£685).Some teachers have expressed concerns about having to enforce the ban.The Green Party's Sigi Maurer accused Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr, from the liberal NEOS, of "creating new conflicts and offloading them onto the teachers".She said teachers were "already under enormous strain" and that Wiederkehr wanted to "foist the role of police officers onto them" on top of their other duties.The opposition far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) says the current ban doesn't go far enough. It is calling for a general prohibition on headscarves and face coverings in schools for students and teachers alike.The FPÖ's Ricarda Berger said there was "no place for political Islam in Austria, and certainly not in our schools".Austria's Chancellor Christian Stocker, leader of the ÖVP, recently called for a constitutional ban on political Islam, telling Austrian public broadcaster ORF he did not "want to live in an Islamic state".In France there has been a ban on wearing any conspicuous religious symbols, including headscarves, turbans and kippas, in schools for more than 20 years.The Austrian law differs from French legislation in that it specifically targets head coverings worn by Muslim women.Austria, like several other European countries including France, Belgium and Denmark, bans the full face veil (niqabs or burkas) in public.Baghajati said the IGGÖ was concerned about "a troubling trend" across Europe "in which complex social challenges are reduced to symbolic measures aimed at minority groups.""Such approaches may generate political attention, but they rarely solve the underlying problems," she said.

schema.headline: Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school

title: Peace talks rich in symbolism but differences between Russia and Ukraine remain
description: Image source, ReutersByDiplomatic correspondentThe talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian
body: Image source, ReutersByDiplomatic correspondentThe talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion. The fact they had to travel by train because they could not risk flying and running the gauntlet of Russian drones - weapons launched on the orders of the man at whose table they sat in the Kremlin only hours ago. The symbolism of Ukrainian President Zelensky greeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's Saint Sophia Cathedral, not only an icon of Ukraine's ancient history, but also just a few yards from where Russian drones hit the headquarters of the country's security services on Friday. You did not have to join too many dots to work out the point Zelensky was making.Both sides held talks for several hours; they were later joined by some European national security advisers, including the UK's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell. And afterwards, all sides spoke warmly of having held substantive discussions. They spoke hopefully of reviving past "trilateral talks" involving both the US and Europe.Image source, ReutersBut fundamental differences remain. The US envoys had come hot foot from Moscow where Vladimir Putin had told them Russia was making "tangible advances" on the battlefield. The story they heard from Ukraine was different, in fact the opposite. Ukrainian officials claim that in August they gained more territory than they lost and Russia suffered 42,000 casualties, dead or wounded.Putin had also told the US envoys the root causes of the conflict had to be addressed, shorthand for his longstanding strategic demands that Ukraine cede territory, abandon hopes of joining Nato and reduce the size of its army.After the talks, Zelensky insisted Ukraine would require "strong and clear" security guarantees, including a strong army. Nor did he give any sign of being willing to give up any territory in the eastern Donbas region, an issue he described dryly as "difficult".Figure caption, Watch: President Zelensky welcomes US envoys in KyivWitkoff insisted progress had been made and the ingredients for a settlement were there. But he admitted both sides would have to make compromises to narrow the differences between them. And right now, it is hard to see either side doing that.So for now, the expectation in Kyiv is that the fighting will continue and they will face a hard winter ahead. Some diplomats talk of a window of opportunity for a possible settlement next spring. Others are less optimistic. Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit because the short-term pause in air strikes agreed by both sides had given the people of Kyiv a brief respite. Few expect it to last for long.Figure caption, Watch: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner say they are "encouraged" by Ukraine talks

schema.headline: Peace talks rich in symbolism but differences between Russia and Ukraine remain

title: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea: Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard shine for Gunners
description: Arsenal shelled out close to £200m on new signings during the summer transfer window but fell short of landing the elite forward they craved.Former Ma
body: Arsenal shelled out close to £200m on new signings during the summer transfer window but fell short of landing the elite forward they craved.Former Manchester City goalscorer Julian Alvarez was on their radar but remains at Atletico Madrid, while the Gunners were also interested in Aston Villa's Morgan Rogers, Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and Vinicius Jr.While Rogers opted for London rivals Chelsea, Barcola moved to Liverpool and Vinicius Jr has stayed at Real Madrid.Yet reigning champions Arsenal have started this season as strongly as they finished 2025-26, when they celebrated their first Premier League title for 22 years.After wins over Coventry City and Aston Villa, they came from behind to beat big-spending Chelsea 2-1 in a thrilling derby on Sunday - thanks to goals from two familiar faces.Kai Havertz, an Arsenal player since 2023, and Martin Odegaard, who joined in 2021, scored as they passed their first big test of the campaign against opponents who have spent close to £350m since the end of last season.A maximum nine points from three games, one goal conceded and big players stepping up."I can't see anyone stopping Arsenal," former Premier League winner Chris Sutton told BBC Sport.It is surely too early in the season to get carried away, and there are likely to be bigger tests ahead for Mikel Arteta's side.But Arsenal have set down an early marker as they chase back-to-back Premier League crowns.Along with Manchester City, they are one of only two clubs with a maximum nine points from three games.After sweeping aside Coventry on the opening day of the season, they produced a mature performance to come away with all three points at Villa.Against Chelsea, they had to find a different way to win after £117m signing Rogers fired Chelsea into a second-minute lead."Our mentality is to keep fighting. We have shown that many times," said captain Odegaard, who scored the 50th-minute winner after Havertz had equalised before half-time."We never want to concede early, but the reaction is top. We got our reward in the end and the response was brilliant."We showed our quality with and without the ball and the result reflects that."Odegaard has scored three goals in four appearances in all competitions this season, after netting only once in 36 last term."It was a big game, massive game, tough opponent, and we got there in the end, so brilliant," he said.Former Manchester United and England player Ashley Young said Odegaard's form will be key for Arsenal this season."He's just a joy to watch," Young told BBC Sport."He's exciting when he gets on the ball, he's allowing other players to get on the ball."The connection down the right side between him, Bukayo Saka and Havertz - it's just good to see when you've got players that know each other and build relationships in that way."Riccardo Calafiori has been brilliant from last season. He seems to me like he's the one that's got a free role in the team."It was his run, and he played it precisely, for the winning goal. He goes quickly, takes people out of the way. It's just clever. Arsenal deserved all three points."Havertz said Odegaard was back to his "very best"."He's an unbelievable player - we have seen that over the last years," said the Germany forward."He's going to help us a lot this season."Sutton said Arsenal are still ahead of the rest, despite their rivals spending hundreds of millions of pounds during the transfer window."They're such a powerhouse," said the former Blackburn and England striker."Chelsea are a good team, but Arsenal always find a way to win. Can you stop Arsenal? I don't think they [other Premier League teams] can."Arsenal have won their opening three games of a top-flight campaign while conceding fewer than two goals (1) for the third time - after 1924-25, when they finished 20th, and 2003-04, when they went the season unbeaten.They have also won eight league games in a row stretching back to last season.Having seen off big-spending Chelsea, their next league match is at Sunderland on Saturday.Before that Arsenal launch their Champions League campaign at Napoli on Wednesday.Havertz said Arsenal will head to Italy with confidence high with after seeing off his former club Chelsea."Chelsea have an amazing squad, but so do we," said Havertz, who scored the winning goal for the Blues against Manchester City in the 2021 Champions League final."We knew it was going to be tough. They scored early, so it's not easy for us, but we believed in ourselves and changed the game around."

schema.headline: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea: Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard shine for Gunners

title: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea: Are Blues short of midfield options despite £349m spent?
description: Chelsea ended Sunday's 2-1 defeat by champions Arsenal with two players who began their careers as right-backs alongside each other in midfield.After
body: Chelsea ended Sunday's 2-1 defeat by champions Arsenal with two players who began their careers as right-backs alongside each other in midfield.After spending £349m during the summer transfer window, how did they reach that point?It was Reece James, who began his career as a right-back, who failed to track captain Martin Odegaard as he scored Arsenal's winner at Emirates Stadium.In the build-up to his first defeat as Chelsea manager, Xabi Alonso said he believes James can become one of the best midfielders in the world.James performed well otherwise and spent almost half of last season playing in midfield.But there are legitimate questions about Chelsea's depth in that area after Malo Gusto replaced midfielder Romeo Lavia in the second half.It was lax marking that led to Odegaard's winner, while a lack of creativity from the bench left Chelsea short as Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta's substitutes ultimately helped guide the hosts to victory."Chelsea don't have European football this season so they're playing less games and can concentrate on the Premier League. But the worry is you're finishing a game against the champions, and you've got two right-backs in midfield," Ashley Young told BBC Sport."You look at Lavia, who was injured a lot last season. The front line are going to send fear throughout the league but behind that you see the midfield and they're playing right-backs there."Teams will be seeing the game today, seeing that Chelsea will sit in there and get men behind the ball, but there's still spaces through the lines, and Arsenal found that out."Chelsea are giving up a lot of possession and they're playing counter-attacking football. Today there was probably only once with [Pedro] Neto down the right side when they capitalised on the counter."The primary issue is the absence of midfielder Moises Caicedo.The Ecuador international is out with an unspecified injury for an unknown period after breaking down just 11 minutes into a substitute appearance against Brighton last week.It has left Alonso in almost uncharted territory for a Chelsea boss. Aside from suspensions, Caicedo had missed only two matches during the previous three seasons, through a knock and illness.Asked about Caicedo, Alonso said: "Not longer term, but it is about assessing the risk. Probably last week we brought him back too early and I don't want to make the same mistake again."It remains unclear whether Chelsea had concerns over Caicedo's fitness while pursuing several central midfielders on transfer deadline day.Monaco pulled the plug on Chelsea's £47m move for Lamine Camara at the last minute, leaving officials at Stamford Bridge furious.Chelsea also had bids of up to £64m rejected for Bournemouth's Alex Scott earlier in the summer and were prevented from signing France international Manu Kone after Roma head coach Gian Piero Gasperini blocked the move.Chelsea said they pursued Camara because of a market opportunity, adding that they were satisfied with their summer business and retained faith in their current options.That was despite selling Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City for a joint British-record fee of £125m on deadline day, without signing a direct replacement.However, Caicedo's absence means he joins Jordan Henderson on the sidelines, with the England international still recovering from a broken arm suffered after falling over an advertising hoarding while an unused substitute at the World Cup.Natural midfielder Valentin Barco, who joined from Strasbourg in the summer, has been overlooked in favour of Gusto in all three of Chelsea's Premier League matches.With Gusto starting in midfield, Chelsea recorded 25.6% possession in last weekend's 4-3 victory over Brighton, their lowest figure since records began in 2003-04.If all of Chelsea's midfield options are fit, and Caicedo's injury proves only minor, they should be able to cope with five midfielders in a season without midweek European football, as Alonso argued before the match.Chelsea have leaned on their star attackers in Morgan Rogers, a resurgent Cole Palmer and the prolific Joao Pedro in their opening three matches. Yet having conceded seven goals in three matches, Alonso said "we want to be tighter".There was still plenty to admire about Chelsea's performance.Club-record signing Rogers scored again in the second minute, becoming the first Chelsea player to score or assist in each of the club's opening three Premier League matches of a season since Eden Hazard in 2018-19.It was arguably one of Chelsea's better performances against Arsenal during a run of 10 matches without a win against their London rivals.There remains a 33-point gap to make up after Chelsea finished 10th in the Premier League last season.Alonso said after the match: "We came to win. We knew that we were not that far, but it went their way. "It hurts, [we're] disappointed for sure. But this is the first defeat, this is going to be a long way and it doesn't have a big impact in our mood and in our mindset."Arsenal remain the benchmark Chelsea are trying to reach. Although the Blues beat them to the signing of Rogers, they still trail the standard-setters in London and the Premier League.It served to highlight that, despite already recruiting 10 first-team players during a busy summer, Chelsea's failure to sign a midfielder on deadline day may have left them with a potential weakness.Alonso described the summer as "phase one" earlier this week. If Caicedo's return does not resolve Chelsea's midfield issues, the club may face questions over its decision not to sign a replacement for Fernandez before turning back to the market in January.

schema.headline: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea: Are Blues short of midfield options despite £349m spent?

title: Andrew Scott feels the Pressure as 'unsung hero' in WW2 thriller
description: Image source, Alex Bailey/Focus Features/StudioCanalImage caption, Andrew Scott plays chief meteorological adviser James Stagg, who advised General Ei
body: Image source, Alex Bailey/Focus Features/StudioCanalImage caption, Andrew Scott plays chief meteorological adviser James Stagg, who advised General Eisenhower during World War TwoByHelen BushbyCulture reporterAndrew Scott says he loved his latest acting role as Group Captain James Stagg, the meteorologist key to the success of World War Two's D-Day - the largest seaborne invasion in history."He may not have been the most charming person, but I think he had a huge amount of humility in the face of nature. And that's one of the themes I think of the film," Scott tells the BBC."He appeared to me to be an extraordinarily interesting cinematic character, as well as an unsung hero from history."Stagg played a crucial advisory role when US General Dwight D Eisenhower invaded Normandy, laying the foundations for the Allied victory in World War Two. "It was a wonderful part to play," he says, while painting a mixed picture of Stagg, calling him "very chilly", while also "forthright, direct, obsessed with weather - and not afraid to speak truth to power". Image source, Met Office National Meteorological Library & ArchiveImage caption, James Stagg was from Dalkeith, near EdinburghStagg isn't a traditional war hero, something Scott clearly relished sinking his acting teeth into. "I really enjoyed the way that Stagg was not interested in ingratiating himself with anybody," he told BBC Culture correspondent David Sillito, calling him "a real fish out of water in this situation".The actor's other starring roles couldn't be more different, including romantic fantasy film All of Us Strangers, for which he was nominated for a Golden Globe, plus his memorable "hot priest" in TV's Fleabag and the menacing Jim Moriarty in Sherlock, for which he won a Bafta. His award-winning stage roles include Vanya and Present Laughter. In Pressure, Stagg is thrown into a high-stakes furnace of egos. He has to work with a team of meteorologists who robustly and publicly disagree with each other. Stagg "wasn't a particularly garrulous character" Scott says, which is partly why he was perhaps an unlikely hero. "So many of the heroes in our own lives don't have that big swashbuckling moment," he says. "And you know, a hero comes in all different shapes and sizes."I tried not to be afraid of the fact that perhaps, at the beginning, the audience might be like, 'Who is this guy?' And hopefully by the end we understand his motivations and his inner workings."Image source, Alex Bailey/StudioCanal SASImage caption, Brendan Fraser (far left) plays General Eisenhower, who led the Allied forces and went on to become US president The actor is speaking to the BBC on board HMS Belfast, which led the opening bombardment for the D-Day landings, when tens of thousands of troops from the UK, the US, Canada and France attacked German forces on the coast of northern France on 6 June 1944.Eisenhower needed a full moon, low tide, not much cloud or wind and low seas, external. "The stakes were so enormously high... they were all locked down, and they couldn't leave the place. Stagg's wife was very heavily pregnant at the time, so it was a very, very difficult time for him," Scott explains.  "It's completely unimaginable, the pressure that they would have been under, not just Stagg, but everybody in the building."This of course explains the name of the film, which is based on the successful 2014 stage play by actor and writer David Haig. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Andrew Scott is pictured on HMS Belfast, which catalogues the true events behind the film in a temporary exhibition  The film also charts how Eisenhower had the good sense to pay heed to the experts around him.Scott says although the film is about many things, it's chiefly about "the humility of leadership, and about the difference between power and expertise"."Real experts have the humility to go, 'I don't know about that, but I am in a position of power, so I'm going to delegate this, and I'm gonna listen to what this person has to say'," he says. The film's co-writer and director, Anthony Maras, employed his own weather experts for the film, including Martin Young, a former deputy chief of the UK's Met [Meteorology] Office, external, who'd spent 40 years studying the weather and more than 10 as its chief forecaster. Young's long career also meant he had first-hand knowledge of processes, data and equipment Stagg would have used. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The real Eisenhower (far left) with British Army General Sir Bernard "Monty" Montgomery (right, played by Damian Lewis in the film)  The film is nearly all set in the planning rooms for D-Day, and you see all of them working around the clock, while living on top of each other. "There's a huge amount of wit in the film that I really enjoyed," Scott says, while adding: "I love films that are about work. "These relationships are no less significant because they're work relationships, they're collegiate. "And at the end of these extraordinary three days they shake hands with each other - he's not a hugger, that probably wasn't part of the culture then. "But they nevertheless went through something absolutely enormous together, and they had enormous feelings towards each other - whether that was rage, admiration, intimidation or connection."Image source, Sweeney familyImage caption, Maureen Sweeney, pictured with her husband Ted, made a crucial phone call from their lighthouse in Ireland, confirming a break in the weatherScott also managed to use some previous experience of working on a film about D-Day to help with his performance. "I've been very lucky. As a young actor, I was in the opening sequence of Saving Private Ryan [Steven Spielberg's Oscar-winning film which depicts the horror, fear and brutality facing troops landing at Normandy]. "I was there for that as a 19-year-old on the beach. So, of course, I have no sense of what the horrorism would have been like as a reality, but I certainly had an idea of how it would have looked visually because he stretched the camera for as long as the eye could see."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Saving Private Ryan, released in 1998,  starred Tom Hanks in a visceral account of what D-Day was likeScott is delighted that Pressure pays tribute not only to Stagg, but also references another unsung hero, Maureen Sweeney, who lived in Ireland and was the first to confirm any break in the weather, from her lighthouse in County Mayo."It's another story in itself actually," Scott adds."A big part of my family are from around those parts. So that was wonderful," the Irish actor adds. Scott ends by saying why he was so drawn to the film, and Stagg in particular."I think there's something just very moving about a singular passion someone might get."Their imagination might get captured by the weather as a young man, and if you apply yourself to something and you become excellent at something, it serves a place in the world and serves a place in humanity."He quietly went back to his life and it's wonderful that we can pay tribute to him in this way all these years later. He's a movie hero."Pressure is in UK and Irish cinemas from 9 September

schema.headline: Andrew Scott feels the Pressure as 'unsung hero' in WW2 thriller

title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks
description: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what ap
body: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board. In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening.""I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film."The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody."Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate. Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics. "They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said. He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy". Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations. He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."Speaking after watching the interview, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: "For a political party that don't like foreigners much they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash."We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them."He added: "I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they're really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going."There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days". They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats. They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029. They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest. Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage. But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.   What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake. One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions". No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty". And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage". Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said. But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say." But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing. Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

schema.headline: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks

title: Indonesia fires: The volunteer firefighters risking their lives to defuse 'carbon bombs'
description: The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs'Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fahrin Ramadhianto has
body: The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs'Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fahrin Ramadhianto has been fighting Borneo's wildfires for a month - and noticing the impacts on his body.ByGavin Butler and Ahmad DhaniReporting fromBanjarbaru, KalimantanThe sky grows heavy in Borneo, though not with rain. The air, amber-hued and treacle-thick, is smudged under a blanket of smog that has spilled across international borders – to Singapore, Manila, Kuala Lumpur. Down on the ground, smoke steams from the soil.It's like tear gas, says Dwi Sujatmoko."It hits your nose straight away, your eyes burn – that's more or less what it's like," he says. "People say these fires are extraordinary because of the flames and the smoke. And they're right."The 35-year-old volunteer firefighter has spent more than a month enveloped in this haze, breathing toxic millennia-old microparticles of carbon as he toils against a seemingly inextinguishable fire front.Using hand tools, carts and portable fire pumps, he and thousands of other volunteer firefighters – many of them indigenous Dayak or Banjar people – are up against an inferno that has carbonised some 200,000 hectares of forest and farmland across Indonesian Borneo since early July. Underground and out of sight, giant subterranean peat fires continue to smoulder, choking the air with poisonous fumes."Once a fire becomes uncontrolled, it harms many people. Not just humans, but also animals and plants," Sujatmoko says. "If underground fire spreads and can no longer be controlled, the losses are enormous."Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fires have torched some 200,000 hectares across Indonesian Borneo since early JulyIndonesia is in the throes of a wildfire catastrophe.Amid a so-called "Super El Niño" that has supercharged local drought conditions, thousands of active fire hotspots are spreading and multiplying across the country, fuelling a transnational haze crisis that is the region's worst in more than a decade.But what makes Borneo's fires particularly worrying is the fact that they are burning through one of the world's largest tropical peatland ecosystems.This 4.5-million-hectare swathe of forest and swamp, under normal conditions, serves as a valuable reservoir for ancient carbon.When these peatlands catch fire, they risk releasing millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane into the atmosphere – a "pulse" of greenhouse gas emissions that has earned them the sobriquet of "carbon bomb"."Peatlands are incredibly effective carbon stores because their waterlogged conditions slow decomposition, allowing carbon to accumulate underground for thousands of years," explains Dr Nisa Novita, a peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN)."But this also means they can become a 'carbon bomb' when they are drained or burned, because that carbon can be rapidly released into the atmosphere."Tropical peatlands in Indonesia are among the world's most effective natural carbon stores. The deeper the peat, the greater the carbon stock – and in Kalimantan, we have found peat deposits that can exceed 20 metres in depth."A peatland that deep has been known to harbour more than 6,000 tonnes of carbon – roughly equivalent to the annual CO₂ emissions of 4,800 cars – per hectare. And when it burns, says Dr Nisa, that fossilised carbon can be released into the atmosphere "very rapidly".Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, "We're doing everything we can to help deal with this haze disaster because it's our duty," says firefighter Dwi SujatmokoThe toxic cloudThousands of people across South East Asia are now feeling the effects of those emissions in their eyes, chests and throats. Across Indonesia as well as Brunei, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines, air pollution indices have soared to "unhealthy" extremes - almost 75 times the World Health Organization's recommended level, in some cases – and hospital admissions have surged.Between July and August, Indonesia's Health Ministry recorded over 50,000 cases of respiratory infections linked to land and forest fires. More than 12,000 of them were children under the age of five."Everybody who's living within that pollution cloud is breathing in the products of those smouldering peat fires," says Susan Page, a professor at the University of Leicester's school of geology and the environment, who's been researching peatlands in Asia for three decades."They're breathing in carbon monoxide, which is toxic, and they're breathing in the very finely divided particulate matter... [which] can pass through the alveoli in the lungs into the bloodstream and cause further problems elsewhere in the body, including issues with the heart."Living in this kind of pollution cloud is extremely unhealthy."Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Fighting peat fires requires saturating the ground so thoroughly that it becomes "like porridge"Nowhere are these health impacts being felt more acutely than at the coalface of the disaster: the fire front.Here, volunteer firefighters have been risking their lives and lungs to extinguish burning peatlands which are notoriously difficult to put out. Two volunteers  in Central Kalimantan have died in recent days, reportedly after their health deteriorated from putting out fires.Cloaked in toxic haze that can burn years off a person's lifespan, volunteers have been digging ponds, canals and borewells through bone-dry peat in a desperate attempt to keep their hoses tapped. Some have been driving pipes into the earth, making ad hoc irrigation systems to combat subterranean fires. Others have been sleeping within a stone's throw of the frontline so they can battle the blazes through the night."The worst thing here has been the smoke," says Fahrin Ramadhianto, a volunteer firefighter in South Kalimantan's Banjarbaru, one of the worst-hit areas. "The smell is like decaying wood being burned – that's the characteristic smell of peat. And that peat contains decomposed wood and organic material from many different sources."An unnatural imbalanceIndonesia's peatland fires are not a new phenomenon. Experts say the crisis is rooted in decades of land-use change, dating back to the Suharto era, when vast areas of rainforest and peatland in Kalimantan were opened for logging, plantations and large-scale development projects.Yet authorities have historically avoided blaming industrial actors for causing large-scale fires. Instead, the same indigenous communities who are now engaged in firefighting operations across the island have often been accused of triggering the blazes, due to traditional farming methods that use controlled burns to clear away vegetation.Tono, a representative of the Dayak Kanayatn people of West Kalimantan, told the BBC that Dayak communities are frequently used as scapegoats, despite carrying out land clearing with extensive planning, caution and adherence to multi-generational customs. Tono says these communities' traditional practices, known as uma bukit or "hill farming", are rooted in the idea of maintaining balance with nature.Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, "The worst thing here has been the smoke," says Fahrin RamadhiantoBut the natural balance is fast unravelling in Kalimantan, the most deforested area in Indonesia. The region lost almost 160,000 hectares of forest area in 2025, more than one-third of the nationwide figure – much of it to make way for plantations and monocrop agriculture.It is these same industrial-scale development projects that have been largely responsible for draining the area's peat swamps, which renders them significantly more fire-prone, Prof Page says."Peatlands aren't really the ideal place to set up a plantation – but of course, once the more suitable mineral soils had been exhausted it became possible, by using large machinery, to drain the peatlands and create conditions which would be dry enough," she says."So not only have you got the deforestation, but peatland drainage of course has also greatly increased the fire risk."Page also points out that, whether on fire or not, a drained peatland emits carbon dioxide into the atmosphere "all of the time"."I think that's forgotten," she says. "I think it's important to recognise that when we see the fires, they're like a dramatic example of what is actually going on the whole time in a drained peatland... The fires are just the worst expression of [that]."Now, as these latest fires continue to spiral out of control, Sujatmoko and others face a concatenation of difficulties in the coming days, weeks and months – not least of which is a shortage of water. Image source, Ahmad Dhani for BBCImage caption, Drainage and drought in Indonesia's peatlands has exacerbated their vulnerability to fire Fighting peat fires requires saturating the ground so thoroughly that it becomes "like porridge", Sujatmoko explains.Even then there is a high chance the fire will reappear, like a smoking revenant, fed by hidden fuel buried in the invisible depths of the peat swamp.In the face of these persistent reignitions, ongoing drought conditions and toxic smog, fatigue is another concern."We're definitely tired," says Sujatmoko. "We get exhausted, we miss our families, our children, our wives. But for now, all of us are putting those things aside. We're doing everything we can to help deal with this haze disaster because it's our duty.""We also hope rain comes soon," he adds. "We've spent months away from home... May all the efforts of those on the front lines be a blessing for everyone."Additional reporting by Faisal Irfani from BBC Indonesian.

schema.headline: Indonesia fires: The volunteer firefighters risking their lives to defuse 'carbon bombs'

title: Maryam Moshiri: BBC News presenter reveals she has blood cancer
description: BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has revealed she is living with blood cancer. Moshiri, who joined the BBC in 2003 and is one of the news channel's b
body: BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has revealed she is living with blood cancer. Moshiri, who joined the BBC in 2003 and is one of the news channel's best-known anchors, told the BBC she wanted to share her diagnosis to raise awareness about the disease. "It's been two years since my diagnosis and I've felt that I've started to understand the disease a lot better and the way it affects my life. I've got a handle on it to a degree now, so I felt it was really important to raise awareness," the 49-year-old said."I'm going to have to spend the rest of my life being treated for this," she added.Moshiri was diagnosed in November 2024 with polycythaemia vera (PV) - a rare, treatable blood cancer. Although it cannot be cured, it can be managed effectively.In PV, your body makes too many red blood cells, which makes the blood thicker than normal.It leads to a higher risk of developing blood clots, which can cause a stroke, heart attack or deep vein thrombosis (DVT).Symptoms can include headaches, confusion, dizziness and blurred vision."I was told by my consultant that I have this incurable blood cancer," she said. "Mostly I had no symptoms and that's one of the problems with this disease."The only reason mine was caught was because my GP was so fastidious in the way she did my routine blood tests and immediately sent them for further diagnosis."As part of her initial treatment, the BBC News chief presenter underwent several "debilitating" hour-long sessions of venesections.Venesection is a procedure where a needle is put into a vein in the arm to slowly draw the blood out. This blood letting can be an effective way to reduce the thickness of the blood. "In about a space of five months, I had venesection seven or eight times. So you can imagine my iron levels hit the floor and I felt even more exhausted," she said. "After a while I started feeling extremely unwell and tired. I started losing my hair, I got itchy all over my body, but the main symptom was fatigue."Later, Moshiri was able to get on an immunotherapy treatment called interferon through the NHS, and after some tweaks, she says she is in a better place."I've only needed one venosection in about 15 months, so that's been really good. The last couple of months have been better than the last two years," she said. "I think it's really important people understand that this blood cancer is incurable but it's manageable with the right treatment and you can lead a relatively healthy life."It's just a question of finding the right treatment and making sure it works for you."She admits she is "not the person I was two years ago" but says she feels "much better". The mother-of-three said she has had to adjust to life with her condition, sometimes not being able to attend family occasions or play with her children because she is exhausted. "It's the kind of fatigue that is not like I'm just tired and I didn't get a good night's sleep, you feel like someone has removed your battery completely, and however much sleep you get makes no difference," she explains. "Even though I feel the best I have in two years, I don't know how I'm going to be in six months, one year, two years. "People with PV have a higher chance of stroke, heart attack or DVT, so it's something I always have be aware of and make sure I mitigate."Despite the fatigue, Moshiri has continued to travel across the world covering the biggest stories over the last two years for the BBC, anchoring from Qatar at the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, covering the selection of the new Pope from the Vatican and travelling to Greenland for Vice-President JD Vance's visit.She credits her "supportive and helpful" husband Jonathan, management at the BBC and her children Iris, 13, Vivienne, 11 and Caspian, 9. "It took me a long time to be able to tell them about this illness, because I don't want to worry them, but they have been so understanding. When I say things like 'mummy is to tired to play with you', they get it and they don't push it," she said. Helen Rowntree, chief executive of Blood Cancer UK, said: "We're so grateful to Maryam for bravely sharing her story. When public figures speak openly about their diagnosis, it cuts through the silence that so often surrounds blood cancer – the UK's fifth most common cancer and third biggest cancer killer."Rowntree said blood cancer can feel like a "silent" cancer as patients can present with vague, hard to spot symptoms, and highlighted that many with the disease manage their illness, treatment and side-effects alongside work and family life. "We urgently need continued public and government support to fund the next generation of kinder, more effective treatments with fewer side-effects – so that more people with blood cancer can live well, spend less time dealing with the impact of treatment and be there for the moments that matter," she added. "There is a lot of research going into blood cancer and scientific advancement to look forward to. Hopefully they'll be some sort of advancement that will help even more than these medications I've been given," Moshiri added.

schema.headline: Maryam Moshiri: BBC News presenter reveals she has blood cancer

title: Chancellor John Healey to say UK economy 'turning a corner' despite debt concerns
description: The chancellor is set to give an upbeat view of the state of the UK economy ahead of next month's Budget, building on a recent uptick in consumer and
body: The chancellor is set to give an upbeat view of the state of the UK economy ahead of next month's Budget, building on a recent uptick in consumer and business confidence.In a speech on Monday, John Healey will talk of a "new story" of the economy not just turning a corner, but being resilient, optimistic and "ready to seize the opportunities of new technologies and ideas". He will also unveil a £150m fund for companies in the north of England.Healey is facing pressures ahead of his first Budget, including concerns about government borrowing costs and inflationary impacts of the Iran war.The Conservatives said Healey's plans would "do little to comfort hard-working families and businesses".The £150m fund is part of a wider plan to generate more economic growth around the UK.Healey will detail plans to use public investment to "unlock private investment, to support our innovation economy, and to create the new jobs their areas need".The fund, from money already allocated to the British Business Bank, will provide investments of between £5m and £15m to the "most innovative and fast-growing firms". It is expected to back university spin-outs and other "ambitious businesses" across the north.Describing a country "turning the corner", the chancellor is expected to say: "The prime minister laid out a clear diagnosis of what has gone wrong in the past. The solution is a fundamental shift that starts with putting power in the right places."The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places."Recent ructions in government debt markets have made constrained public finances worse, with the Treasury needing to fill possible multi-billion pound gaps caused by rising borrowing costs, and the need to fund higher defence spending.As he prepares to deliver his Budget on 28 October, the chancellor says he is as committed to balancing the books as his predecessor.But the tone matters, and to get high saving consumers spending, and cautious businesses investing, Downing Street wants to point to sunnier times ahead for now, more than the prospect of tough Budgetary medicine.Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Economic growth in every postcode sounds great and is something we would all love. I think it'll actually be much harder to achieve in practice."She said it would be easier to see how the government could make stronger second and third cities than to see "how it would drive growth in literally every postcode".During his first Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, Andy Burnham faced scrutiny over rising UK borrowing costs. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged him to say how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK reached a new 18-year high.Burnham blamed the previous Tory administration, and said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility".Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said Healey's plan would do "little to comfort hard-working families and businesses across the country who are worried about more tax rises or the fact that government borrowing rates are near a 28-year high".He added: "We are facing serious threats from Russia and Iran on our doorstep, as well as threats to the Falkland Islands."Yet the chancellor, the man who resigned over defence spending, seemingly does not want to mention our armed forces or how we will reach 3% of GDP on defence."Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "Re-announcing £150m across the entire north of England will barely shift the dial on growth."Robert Jenrick, Reform UK's economic spokesman, said: "Days after a market meltdown, when grip and direction are required, John Healey has revealed himself to be an empty vessel with no idea about how to rescue our economy."

schema.headline: Chancellor John Healey to say UK economy 'turning a corner' despite debt concerns

title: Germany's far-right AfD set for big win in eastern state, just short of majority
description: Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) is heading for a dramatic victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of its mainstream rivals. A
body: Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) is heading for a dramatic victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of its mainstream rivals. Although it is projected to fall short of a majority, the AfD says it has won a mandate to govern.The far-right AfD is on course to win a record 44% of the vote, well ahead of the conservative CDU on 17%, with most interim results counted.Charismatic leader in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, said it was "sensational" and they wanted to start governing as soon as possible.No far-right party has won control of a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing, local education and culture.Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.He along with joint national leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla were overjoyed as exit polls revealed they were on track to score more than double the party's result in 2021.Commentators and political opponents spoke of the outcome as a watershed and break with the past. Main TV channel Das Erste cancelled its legendary crime drama Tatort to focus on what the result meant."This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the German TV projection on his Truth Social platform, and then Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD". Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.Polish centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk saw the result very differently, saying "in Poland only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD".A crowd of supporters at the AfD election night party HQ erupted in cheers as the projections came up on the screen.A short while later, people burst into singing Germany's national anthem."We have made history in this state," Siegmund said. His opposite number in the CDU, Sven Schulze, conceded victory as he watched the conservative vote slump by more than half on the previous election."This was an extremely tough and intensive election campaign," said Schulze, adding that his party would have to deal with the result.Germany's centre-left SPD described the outcome as "truly dramatic" and national leader Lars Klingbeil, whose party is in government nationally with the CDU, described the outcome as a "signal to Berlin" and he was adamant that they would hear it.The anti-migration AfD stands for Alternative für Deutschland. It has not only dominated the election campaign, it is emerging as the dominant force in the result and its supporters believe they are on the march.Turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was particularly high at 76.7%, and AfD supporters in Magdeburg praised Siegmund's success in winning over voters.One man called Ollie said: "This man gives us what no-one else can give.""No matter what government, they all just promise things to get better. This is a party for the working people. It is the alternative for Germany," he told the BBC.Another AfD voter called Bert said people in the east could sense things were not going well: "Things need to improve for us, for my family - I have three children. I'm in fear, I'm really in fear that safety erodes more and more."Other parties refuse to go into coalition with the AfD, operating a Brandmauer or firewall aimed at keeping the far right out of government. In Saxony-Anhalt, the BSW has offered to co-operate with the AfD on some issues if it gets into the state parliament.The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states. They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. It would not be able to achieve either if it ran the government of one of 16 states.But it would have significant local powers. The party has been particularly critical of the Bauhaus school of design which the Nazis shut down in the city of Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt after they came to power in 1933. The AfD has called it "the dead-end of modernism", prompting some to accuse the party of using similar language to the Nazis.Nikita, a demonstrator at an anti-AfD "Democracy Festival" in Magdeburg on the eve of the vote said Germans had to "learn from our history and not go back. We don't want the dark times any more".Responding to the news from Saxony-Anhalt, the veteran head of the Jewish community in Munich and Bavaria, Charlotte Knobloch, said it frightened her. "On days like this I find it hard to recognise my homeland any more," the 93-year-old Holocaust survivor said, appealing for mainstream parties not to stand by and allow "this decline".One of the AfD's top figures in Saxony-Anhalt, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, has also been criticised for his approach to Russia. When asked why he had a Russian army mug in his office, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war".

schema.headline: Germany's far-right AfD set for big win in eastern state, just short of majority

title: The £70 refund letter that isn't a scam
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentYou may be among the one million people, mostly women, who will receive letters explaining how
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentYou may be among the one million people, mostly women, who will receive letters explaining how you are eligible for top-up pension payments - and it's not a scam.Those entitled are low earners who have missed out on the money because of the way their pension is administered.HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) will write to people over the next few months, explaining how to receive the payment. Typically they will be due £70, but that may vary considerably depending on their circumstances.Anyone eligible will be contacted automatically but, if you receive a letter, there are various checks you can do to ensure the letter is genuine so you don't get hoodwinked.What's the letter about?When you pay into a pension, the government allows some of the money that would otherwise have been paid in tax to go towards your pension instead. This is known as tax relief, external.For relatively complicated reasons, some low earners whose employer used what's known as a Net Pay Arrangement pension scheme received less than those whose pension was administered through a Relief at Source scheme.Employees have no control over the type of scheme that's used, so the government has decided to top up those who have missed out, through what's called a low earner's pension payment.Typically, they would have earned close to, but not more than, £12,570 a year (the starting point for paying income tax).Top-up payments will initially be paid for the 2024-25 tax year, with automated payments subsequently kicking in for later years.  How can I check the letter is for real?Customers don't need to apply. If eligible, you'll be sent information by HMRC - the UK's tax authority - in a letter or through your online personal tax account, external.HMRC will not text, email or call you about it. If you receive such a call or message, it is a scam. Also, it will never ask you to transfer money, or ask for PIN codes or passwords.Other ways to check contact is smooth and genuine include:Making sure HMRC has your latest addressSearching Gov.uk for "check if a letter you've received from HMRC is genuine", and look for "Low Earner's Pension Payment"HMRC also has advice on spotting a scam, externalCustomers will be asked to provide their bank details through their personal tax account. Customers who are digitally excluded will be able to phone HMRC to accept their payment instead"We know some people may be cautious about unexpected contact, which is why we provide clear information about what to expect and how to verify the contact is genuine," said a HMRC spokesman."Customers can check a letter is genuine on Gov.uk and should only respond via official HMRC channels."Is everyone expected to get paid?Sir Steve Webb, partner at pensions consultancy LCP and a former pensions minister, said he was shocked at how few people the government expected to actually receive the payment.The government has estimated the cost of the project to be much lower than if everyone who was eligible took up the payment."The process of getting these payments to the right people is going to be incredibly painful and there is a real risk of huge non take-up," he said.  "It is vital that communications are effective to make sure that people get the money to which they are entitled."HMRC says it will run an awareness campaign using social media and other channels.

schema.headline: The £70 refund letter that isn't a scam
